h1: Plastic bucket or glass carboy or stainless fermenter for homebrew
title: Bucket, Carboy or Stainless Fermenter | Craft Beer School
desc: Plastic bucket, glass carboy, PET or stainless steel fermenter? The real pros and cons of each for homebrewing in India, from cost to cleaning.
teaser: Every fermenter makes beer. The question is which one you will still be happy with after twenty batches.
standfirst: Choosing a fermenter is one of the first real decisions a homebrewer makes. Here is how plastic buckets, glass carboys, PET and stainless steel compare on cost, cleaning, oxygen and safety.
sections: What a fermenter has to do

A fermenter holds wort while yeast turns it into beer. It needs to be food-safe, easy to clean, sealable with an airlock and big enough to leave headspace for krausen. Beyond that, the material decides how easy your life is.

Food-grade plastic buckets, usually HDPE, are where most homebrewers start. Our homebrewing starter kit guide includes one for good reason.

  • Pros: cheap, light, unbreakable, with a wide opening that makes cleaning and adding fruit or dry hops easy. Many come with a tap.
  • Cons: soft plastic scratches easily. Scratches can harbour bacteria. Plastic lets small amounts of oxygen through over time, which matters only for long ageing. Lids do not always seal tightly.

Clean buckets with a soft cloth only, never a scrubbing pad. Replace them every couple of years or sooner if they are scratched or stained. Make sure any bucket you buy locally is food grade, not one meant for paint or chemicals.

Glass carboys, narrow-necked jars of 19 to 23 litres, were the classic upgrade.

  • Pros: glass does not scratch, does not absorb smells and lets no oxygen through. You can watch fermentation happen.
  • Cons: heavy, slippery when wet and dangerous if dropped. The narrow neck makes cleaning harder and dry hopping awkward. Glass also shatters with sudden temperature changes.

If you use glass, carry it in a crate or a harness, never by the neck. Our first homebrew mistakes guide has more on handling.

PET plastic carboys look like glass but weigh far less and do not shatter. They let in less oxygen than HDPE buckets. They cannot take hot liquids, so cool wort before transfer. They still need gentle cleaning.

Some PET fermenters are designed to handle pressure, often up to around 2 bar depending on the model. Those allow closed transfers and pressure fermentation, a big step up for hoppy beers and lagers. Check the rated pressure in the manual and never exceed it.

Stainless steel buckets and small conical fermenters are what many homebrewers aim for eventually.

  • Pros: tough, scratch-resistant, easy to clean with hot water and caustic. They last for decades. Conicals let you dump yeast and trub from the bottom. Some are pressure-rated.
  • Cons: expensive, especially imported models with duties added. You cannot see inside. Cheap stainless with poor welds can be harder to clean than good plastic.

Look for food-grade 304 stainless with smooth, polished welds. Rough welds on the inside are where bacteria hide.

• Cost and availability. Food-grade buckets are easy to find locally. Glass carboys, PET fermenters and stainless conicals are mostly imported and more expensive.
  • Temperature. Without temperature control, the fermenter material makes little difference to temperature. Stainless loses heat a little faster in a water bath, which can help in summer.
  • Space. If you ferment in a fridge, measure the inside before buying. A conical with legs may not fit.

Headspace is easy to overlook. For a 20 litre batch, look for a fermenter of at least 25 litres, ideally 30. Warm Indian ferments throw a big krausen. A full fermenter will push foam and yeast out through the airlock. A blow-off tube into a jar of sanitiser solves it for the first few days.

Taps are worth a thought too. A tap near the bottom makes sampling and bottling easier, but it is one more part to strip and clean. Take it apart after every batch. Beer trapped in a tap body is a common source of infection.

For a first fermenter, a food-grade plastic bucket with a lid and airlock is hard to beat. It is cheap and forgiving. If you brew regularly and want to reduce oxygen pickup, add a PET pressure fermenter. Move to stainless when you are sure brewing is a long-term hobby and you want something that will last.

Many brewers end up with more than one. A bucket for fruit beers and experiments, a pressure fermenter for hoppy beers. Whatever you choose, how you clean it matters more than what it is made of. Our guide on cleaning vs sanitising covers that. A good fermenter is the vessel. Knowing how to run a clean, controlled fermentation in it is the skill.
faqs: Is a plastic bucket good enough for homebrewing?
Yes. A food-grade bucket with a good lid and airlock makes excellent beer. Replace it when it is scratched or stained.
They can be. A full carboy is heavy and slippery. Broken glass causes serious cuts. Carry it in a crate or harness, never by the neck.
Is a stainless fermenter worth the money?
If you brew often and want something that lasts decades and cleans easily, yes. For a first few batches, a plastic bucket is fine.
